Definition: What proportion of businesses does the register cover?
Comments: No direct proportion of all businesses registered for tax was found; IMF PFM blog notes URA registered over 350,000 informal taxpayers by 2022 and EFRIS focuses on VAT-registered businesses, implying overall business taxpayer coverage remains low relative to total enterprises (many informal), assessed as <20%.
revision_notes: The originally cited IMF PFM blog post does not state a proportion of businesses registered for tax; it only notes that URA had registered over 350,000 informal taxpayers via TREP by 2022, which is not a coverage ratio and cannot on its own support a <20% score. Fresher, more direct data: URA's FY2024/25 Annual Data Book (reported by CEO East Africa, May 2026) records 246,799 registered non-individual (business) taxpayers, up from 166,783 in FY2021/22. URSB (the companies registrar) reported a cumulative stock of over 800,000 registered formal business entities by mid-2022 (Business Focus, July 2022), growing by roughly 50,000-70,000 new registrations a year since (URSB Annual Report 2023/24), implying a formal business stock of around 900,000-950,000 by 2025. Dividing URA's non-individual taxpayer count by this estimated formal business stock gives coverage of roughly 25-30%, i.e. the 20-49% band rather than <20%. The denominator is genuinely uncertain, however: URSB's cumulative total includes many dormant or closed entities, and URA's non-individual count includes NGOs and government bodies as well as companies, so the true ratio could plausibly sit either side of the 20% threshold. Recalculated to 2 (20-49%) on this evidence but flagged for human review given the denominator uncertainty.
revised_comments: Uganda Revenue Authority (URA) data for FY2024/25 records 246,799 registered non-individual (business) taxpayers, up from 166,783 four years earlier, reflecting sustained expansion of the tax register through initiatives such as the Tax Registration Expansion Programme. Comparing this to the Uganda Registration Services Bureau's cumulative stock of formally registered business entities, which exceeded 800,000 by 2022 and continues to grow by tens of thousands of registrations annually, suggests that roughly a quarter to a third of formally registered businesses hold an active tax registration. Uganda's economy remains heavily informal - informal enterprises made up around 82% of all businesses in the 2019/20 Census of Business Establishments - which continues to constrain the effective tax base despite growth in the URA register.

Definition: What proportion of individual taxpayers does the register cover?
Comments: No direct national share of individual taxpayers registered was found; IMF PFM blog notes URA registered over 350,000 informal taxpayers by 2022, which is small relative to Uganda's population, suggesting low individual taxpayer coverage (<20%).
revision_notes: The originally cited IMF PFM blog post does not give a national share of individual taxpayers registered; comparing an absolute count of 350,000 informal taxpayers registered by 2022 to Uganda's total population is not the correct denominator (the metric specifies the eligible individual taxpayer base, not total population) and cannot on its own support a <20% score. Fresher, more direct data: URA's FY2024/25 Annual Data Book shows 5.01 million registered individual taxpayers, up from 2.45 million in FY2021/22 (CEO East Africa, May 2026). Uganda's 2024 Population and Housing Census puts the labour force at 11 million and total employment at 9.7 million (Ministry of Finance Macroeconomic & Fiscal Performance Report FY2024/25); the FY2026/27 Budget Speech cites total employment (formal, private and informal) of 13.3 million, and the World Bank's broader labour force estimate is 22.8 million. Against these denominators, 5.01 million registered individual taxpayers implies coverage of roughly 22-52%, consistently above the <20% originally assessed and mostly within the 20-49% band. The correct denominator (registered vs 'active' taxpayers; narrow labour force vs broader employment estimate) is not authoritatively settled, so recalculated to 2 (20-49%) but flagged for human review.
revised_comments: Uganda Revenue Authority (URA) data for FY2024/25 records 5.01 million registered individual taxpayers, more than double the 2.45 million recorded four years earlier, reflecting an aggressive registration drive including the Tax Registration Expansion Programme and the instant Taxpayer Identification Number system. Measured against Uganda's labour force of around 11 million (2024 Population and Housing Census) or total employment estimates of 9.7-13.3 million, this implies that a substantial minority to roughly half of the working population now holds a tax identification number, although the Auditor General's Report notes that only a portion of registered taxpayers are actively filing and paying. Uganda's large informal sector, which accounts for more than half of GDP and over 80% of employment, remains the primary constraint on converting registration into active taxpayer compliance.
